chunks: And by this chain of narration, from Ahmad ibn Abi Abdillah, from Muhammad ibn Ali al-Kufi, from Ali ibn al-Nu'man, from Abdullah ibn Talha, from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) who said:

A servant will not enter Paradise if in his heart is the weight of a mustard seed of pride, nor will a servant enter Hell if in his heart is the weight of a mustard seed of faith. I said, 'May I be your ransom, a man wears clothes and rides a mount, and he almost recognizes pride in himself.' He said, 'That is not pride. Indeed, pride is the rejection of the truth, and faith is the acknowledgment of the truth.'

key_terms.جُعِلْتُ فِدَاكَ: May I be your ransom (a common phrase of respect in hadith)
key_terms.مِثْقَالُ ذَرَّةٍ: Weight of a tiny seed (mustard seed)

ai.seo_question: What is the difference between external pride and true pride in Shia hadith?
ai.summary: In this hadith from *Thawab al-Amal*, Imam al-Sadiq (peace be upon him) distinguishes between superficial arrogance and the spiritual root of *kibr* (pride), defining it specifically as the rejection of truth (*inkar al-haqq*). This clarification aligns with Shia exegetical tradition, which often interprets pride not merely as ego but as a cognitive refusal to acknowledge divine reality, thereby linking it directly to the essence of faith (*iman*) as acceptance. The narration serves as a practical diagnostic tool for believers to examine their internal stance toward truth rather than focusing solely on external displays of status.
